title: Why he told stories
hookLine: Jesus rarely explained himself; he told a short story and let it sit with people (Mark 4:33–34)
carry: a story carries what a lecture can't

lines: A BOAT. A CROWD ON THE SHORE.
A FARMER WENT OUT TO SOW.
cards: A lake in Galilee, early in the day. The crowd is so big the teacher can't stand on the beach anymore. So he climbs into a fishing boat, pushes off, and sits in it, while the whole crowd stands at the water's edge.
Farmers. Fishermen. Mothers with children on their hips.
People who came because a neighbor said you have to hear this man. What does he give them? Not a lecture.
Not a list of rules. He says: listen. A farmer went out to sow.

teach.b: Parable comes from the Greek parabole: something thrown alongside. You throw a small, ordinary picture alongside something too big to look at straight. A seed.
A lost coin. A party. Behind it sits a Hebrew word teachers already used, mashal, which covers proverbs, riddles and short stories.

teach.h: AS THEY WERE ABLE TO HEAR IT.
teach.b: In the King James: "And with many such parables spake he the word unto them, as they were able to hear it. But without a parable spake he not unto them." As they were able to hear it.
That's the first thing a parable does: it meets people where they are. A farmer knows seed. A woman who has swept a floor knows what it is to lose a coin.
Nobody needs a degree to walk in. Second, it stays. A rule is forgotten by lunch.
A shepherd walking into the dark after one sheep follows you home, and you're still turning it over on Tuesday. Third, the twist. Somebody gets paid too much.
The wrong man turns out to be the good one. You have to decide what you think, and sometimes the story turns round and asks where you're standing.
Mark adds one more thing: alone with his closest followers, he explained it all.

teach.h: A STORY STAYS. A RULE FADES.
teach.b: The crowd got the story; the students got the story and the questions.

teach.h: THE TWIST ASKS WHERE YOU STAND.
teach.b: Christians often read the parables as something to live with, not just solve. Some take under a minute to read. The next two weeks are those stories, one a day.

how: Christians read and hear the parables in church, where a Gospel passage is often read aloud and preachers return to them. Some also read one slowly at home and think about it through the day.

o: a short everyday story set beside a bigger truth
a short prayer said aloud during worship
a true account of something that really happened

games.q: what's inside the word — tap the pairs.
p: a Hebrew proverb, riddle or story

s: Jesus mostly taught in long speeches with rules
Mark says without a parable he spoke not unto them. the stories were how he taught.
parable comes from a Greek word meaning thrown alongside
parabole: a small picture thrown alongside something too big to look at straight.
the parables were a brand-new way to teach
Jewish teachers already used the mashal: proverbs, riddles, short stories. Jesus used it again and again.

games.q: a crowd presses you so hard to the water's edge that you can't stand on the beach. you want to teach them. what do you do?
o: send them home and teach tomorrow.
get into a boat, sit in it, and tell a story.
read them a list of rules.
games.why: he sat in a boat on the lake and said: a farmer went out to sow. then he let the story sit, unexplained.

practice: Get comfortable and bring back a story you love: a film, a book, something your grandmother told you. Tell yourself the whole thing in one sentence: not a summary of the plot, its heart.
Then say it again, shorter, and notice why it has stayed with you.

wordCard.voice: Parable. A small, ordinary story thrown alongside something too big to look at straight.

orig.note: Greek. para, beside, plus ballo, to throw: a picture thrown alongside the real thing.
